name: Neck Crank
summary: The Neck Crank is a cervical-spine compression submission, most often applied from Twister Control, that forces the tap by levering the opponent's head into rotation and flexion beyond the neck's safe range while the body pins their torso.
description: Master the Neck Crank submission in BJJ — a cervical-spine compression applied from Twister Control that forces the tap through progressive spinal pressure.
overview:
The Neck Crank is a cervical spine compression submission applied primarily from Twister Control. Unlike chokes that target the carotid arteries or trachea, the neck crank generates a tap through direct mechanical pressure on the cervical vertebrae and surrounding musculature. The attacker uses the body triangle to lock the opponent's torso in place while applying lateral or rotational force to the head, creating a shearing effect on the spine that becomes rapidly unbearable.

This submission occupies a unique space in the grappling hierarchy. While some competition rulesets restrict or ban neck cranks, they remain a legitimate and high-percentage finish in no-gi grappling, particularly from twister control where the opponent's movement is severely limited. The key strategic advantage of the neck crank is that it requires less precision than many other submissions—once the body is locked and the head is controlled, the finishing mechanics are straightforward. However, this same potency demands exceptional training discipline, as the cervical spine is vulnerable to permanent injury when force is applied carelessly.

From a game planning perspective, the neck crank pairs naturally with the twister and banana split as finishing threats from the truck position. The defender must choose which attack to prioritize defending, and each defensive commitment opens vulnerability to the others. Advanced practitioners use the neck crank as both a primary finish and a setup tool to create submission chains from twister control.

injury_risks.injury: Cervical disc herniation or vertebral fracture from excessive rotational force
Neck muscle strain or ligament sprain from sudden force application
injury_risks.recovery_time: 2-6 weeks with rest and physical therapy

injury_risks.injury: Cervical nerve compression causing radiating pain or numbness in extremities

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW AND PROGRESSIVE ONLY. Never apply explosive or jerking force to the cervical spine. Increase pressure gradually over several seconds, giving the defender adequate time to recognize danger and tap. The cervical spine provides minimal warning before catastrophic failure.
tap_signals: Physical tap on partner's body, legs, or the mat (minimum two distinct taps)
Verbal submission ('tap', 'stop', or any verbal indication of distress)
Any sign of distress including grunting, gasping, or going limp—treat as an immediate tap
release_protocol: Release ALL pressure immediately and completely upon any tap signal—do not 'finish the rep'
Gently return the opponent's head to neutral alignment before disengaging the body triangle
Check on your training partner verbally after every neck crank attempt, even if they did not tap
training_restrictions: Prohibited for white and blue belts in most academies; purple belt and above with instructor supervision recommended
Never apply full force in training—use controlled progressive pressure at 50-70% intensity maximum
Do not drill on partners with pre-existing cervical spine injuries, neck surgery history, or active neck pain

variations_and_setups.description: Thread the top arm under the opponent's chin and lock a chin strap grip. Pull the head laterally while the body triangle anchors the torso. This is the highest-percentage variation because the grip under the jaw provides maximum rotational leverage on the cervical spine.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you can access the chin and thread your arm underneath—the default finishing grip from twister control

variations_and_setups.description: Place the palm on the opponent's forehead or crown and push the head forward and down, compressing the cervical spine into flexion rather than rotation. This bypasses chin tuck defenses entirely since the force direction works regardless of jaw position.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent tucks the chin aggressively to block the chin strap grip

variations_and_setups.description: Drive the forearm across the opponent's jaw from the side, creating lateral cervical flexion. The forearm blade sits on the jawline and the pulling direction is perpendicular to the spine. Effective as a transition grip when switching between crank angles.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When traditional chin access is blocked but the jaw remains exposed from the side

attacker.name: Neck Crank Attacker
attacker.description: Finish the Neck Crank from Twister Control. Learn chin-strap mechanics, head control, finishing angles, and the mandatory safety protocol for this cervical lock.
attacker.overview: As the attacker, the Neck Crank from Twister Control is a control-first finish: you must own the opponent's torso through the truck and trapped leg before ever reaching for the head. The submission lives or dies on the foundation underneath it—boot pressure and the figure-four leg trap keep the spine rotated so that when you secure a chin strap or forehead frame, the head has nowhere to follow except into the crank. Because the cervical spine offers almost no warning before failure, every finishing rep is governed by slow, progressive pressure and instant release on the tap, making discipline as important as mechanics.
key_principles: Control precedes the crank—secure the leg trap and chest pressure before reaching for the head
The rotation is built by the lower body; the head control simply harvests torque the twist already created
Combine rotation and flexion rather than pulling the head straight back, which only strains muscle
Boot pressure on the hip keeps the opponent from squaring up and aligning their spine to neutralize the lock
Apply pressure slowly and progressively—the cervical spine gives minimal warning before catastrophic failure
Keep the crank as one threat in a fork with the twister, calf slicer, and back take to force defensive dilemmas
Release instantly and completely on any tap signal—never finish the rep on a neck submission
setup_requirements: Established Twister Control or truck with at least one of the opponent's legs trapped in a figure-four
Constant chest-to-back pressure keeping the opponent flattened on their side and unable to square up
Boot (foot) pressure against the hip generating spinal rotation through the opponent's torso
Clear access to the head or jaw on the side toward which you intend to rotate and flex the neck
Awareness of the ruleset—confirm neck cranks are legal before committing to the finish

execution_steps.action: Consolidate the leg trap and chest pressure
execution_steps.description: Lock the figure-four on the trapped leg and drive your chest into the opponent's back so they cannot square their hips or align their spine, building the stable base the crank requires.

execution_steps.action: Maximize spinal rotation with boot pressure
execution_steps.description: Press your boot into the opponent's hip to twist their lower body away while their shoulders rotate toward you, pre-loading the cervical spine so the finishing grip has immediate leverage.

execution_steps.action: Clear and thread for the head
execution_steps.description: Reach your top arm over the far shoulder toward the chin or jawline, sliding under the head while keeping your elbow tight so the opponent cannot frame into the gap you create.
Cup the jaw with your hand and connect your second hand behind the head with a gable or S-grip, forming a rigid frame around the skull that turns your whole upper body into the cranking lever.
Drive your shoulders and hips to widen the gap between the rotated torso and the head, aligning the lever so that small movements translate into large, controllable force on the cervical spine.
Pull the head toward your chest while combining rotation with forward flexion, increasing pressure gradually over several seconds and reading the opponent for the tap at every increment.
Elevate your hips or arch slightly to feed additional, measured compression into the lock once the grip and angle are set, escalating only as fast as the opponent can recognize and respond.
The instant any tap, verbal signal, or sign of distress appears, release all pressure, return the head to neutral alignment, and check on your partner before disengaging the entanglement.

common_counters.counter: Aggressive chin tuck to deny the chin-strap thread
common_counters.your_response: Switch to the forehead-push crank, attacking flexion instead of rotation since that vector works regardless of jaw position

common_counters.counter: Two-on-one hand fight to peel the cranking arm
common_counters.your_response: Pin the wrist, re-thread, or abandon the crank and climb to traditional back control to keep the dominant position

common_counters.counter: Granby roll toward you to unwind the spinal rotation
common_counters.your_response: Follow the roll and re-insert hooks or chase the back rather than fighting the momentum, accepting guard-top if the position resets

common_counters.counter: Bridging into you to flatten out and reduce torque
common_counters.your_response: Re-establish boot pressure and tighten the leg trap to restore rotation before re-attacking the head

common_errors.error: Applying the crank explosively or with a jerking motion
common_errors.consequence: Severe risk of permanent cervical injury to your partner and likely disqualification under most rulesets
common_errors.correction: Always increase pressure slowly and progressively, giving the defender time to recognize danger and tap

common_errors.error: Reaching for the head before the leg trap and chest pressure are secured
common_errors.consequence: The opponent squares their hips and escapes the position entirely during your reach
common_errors.correction: Finish the foundation first—control the torso and trapped leg, then attack the head last

common_errors.error: Pulling the head straight back without rotation or flexion
common_errors.consequence: You strain the neck muscles without loading the spine, producing a low-percentage attempt the opponent rides out
common_errors.correction: Combine rotation and flexion off the twist the lower body already created for true cervical leverage

common_errors.error: Rising off the opponent's back and losing chest pressure
common_errors.consequence: Space opens for the opponent to turn, breathe, and begin a roll or hip escape
common_errors.correction: Stay heavy with constant chest-to-back connection throughout the entire finishing sequence

common_errors.error: Fixating only on the neck crank and ignoring the fork
common_errors.consequence: A committed defender stalls the single threat while you burn energy on an unavailable angle
common_errors.correction: Chain the crank with the twister, calf slicer, and back take so defending one attack opens another

common_errors.error: Letting the boot pressure lapse during the finish
common_errors.consequence: Spinal rotation collapses, the opponent aligns their spine, and the lock loses all its leverage
common_errors.correction: Maintain boot pressure on the hip the entire time—it is the engine of the rotation the crank depends on

training_progressions.description: Drill threading the chin strap and setting the finishing angle on a fully compliant partner, with zero pressure, until the grip and body alignment are automatic.
With a compliant partner, practice introducing slow, incremental pressure and releasing instantly on the tap, calibrating how little movement produces a response on the cervical spine.
From established Twister Control, work to establish the crank against a defending partner who is allowed to hand-fight and reduce rotation, but never apply fast finishing force.
Integrate the crank into live rounds as part of the twister, calf slicer, and back-take fork, maintaining strict safety discipline and immediate release at all times.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structure does the neck crank attack?
flashcards.answer: The neck crank attacks the cervical spine—the vertebrae of the neck and surrounding musculature—by forcing rotation and flexion beyond the safe range, rather than compressing arteries or the trachea like a choke.

flashcards.question: What must be secured before you ever reach for the opponent's head?
flashcards.answer: You must first secure the leg trap and constant chest-to-back pressure so the torso is locked and the spine is rotated; reaching for the head before this lets the opponent square up and escape.

flashcards.question: How do you know you have reached the finishing position for the crank?
flashcards.answer: The opponent's spine is rotated by your boot pressure, their head is controlled in a rigid chin-strap or forehead frame, and they can no longer realign their spine to neutralize the lever.

flashcards.question: Once the chin strap and rotation are locked, when has the opponent's escape window closed?
flashcards.answer: The escape window effectively closes once the grip locks and rotation is maximized—before that they can hand-fight or roll, but after it the only safe option is to tap.

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks the chin hard to block the chin strap—what grip adjustment do you make?
flashcards.answer: Switch to the forehead-push crank, placing the palm on the forehead or crown and driving the head into flexion, which works regardless of jaw position and bypasses the chin tuck entirely.

flashcards.question: Why is pulling the head straight back an ineffective finishing error?
flashcards.answer: Pulling straight back only strains the neck muscles without loading the cervical spine; the lock needs combined rotation and flexion off the existing twist to generate true mechanical leverage.

flashcards.question: Why must the neck crank always be applied slowly and progressively?
flashcards.answer: The cervical spine gives almost no warning before catastrophic failure, so explosive force can cause permanent injury; slow application gives the defender time to recognize danger and tap safely.

flashcards.question: Your opponent postures up and tries to align their spine—what adjustment prevents the escape?
flashcards.answer: Re-establish boot pressure on the hip and tighten the figure-four leg trap to restore spinal rotation and break their posture before re-attacking the head, denying the alignment they need.

flashcards.question: What body action incrementally increases compression once the grip is set?
flashcards.answer: Elevating the hips or arching into a controlled bridge feeds additional, measured compression into the lock once the grip and angle are established—escalated only as fast as the partner can respond.

flashcards.question: In a ruleset that bans neck cranks, how should you still use the threat?
flashcards.answer: Use it as a positional threat rather than a finish—the defender's reaction to the crank opens the legal twister, calf slicer, or back take—and always confirm legality before applying any pressure.

defender.name: Neck Crank Defender
defender.description: Defend and escape the Neck Crank from Twister Control. Learn recognition cues, neck protection, rotation reduction, escapes, and early-tap safety.
defender.overview: Defending the Neck Crank begins the moment you sense your spine being rotated and your head levered from Twister Control—long before the finishing grip arrives. Your survival hierarchy is fixed: protect the neck first with a tight chin tuck and a two-on-one on the cranking arm, then attack the foundation by freeing the trapped leg and flattening your hips to kill the rotation that powers the lock. Panic and explosive bridging only feed torque into your own cervical spine, so escapes are calm, sequential, and timed to the windows the attacker gives you. Above all, recognize the point where escape is gone and tap early—the neck is never worth a long-term injury.
key_principles: Protect the neck first—chin tuck and hand-fight the cranking arm before attempting any escape
Address the trapped leg as the foundation; freeing it lets you realign your spine and kill the rotation
Reduce spinal rotation before any explosive movement—moving while fully twisted increases torque on your neck
Stay calm and breathe; panic burns the energy you need for a sequential escape and worsens the position
Time escapes to the attacker's transitions, when grips and pressure briefly loosen
Deny the chin strap by keeping your chin glued to your chest and your jaw inaccessible
Recognize the point of no escape and tap early—cervical safety outranks positional pride
recognition_cues: An arm threading across your jaw or under your chin toward a chin-strap grip
Your head being levered away from your shoulders while your torso is held in place
Rotational pressure building through your neck and upper spine as the boot twists your hips
Heavy chest-to-back pressure pinning you on your side and preventing you from squaring up

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one hand fight on the cranking arm plus a hard chin tuck
defensive_options.when_to_use: The instant you feel the arm threading for your chin or jaw
defensive_options.if_successful: Denies the chin-strap grip and removes the lever, stalling the finish
defensive_options.risk: Committing both hands can briefly expose you to a grip switch or back-take pressure

defensive_options.action: Granby roll toward the direction of rotation to recover guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: Before the finishing grip fully locks, while the rotation is still partial
defensive_options.if_successful: You roll through the twist and recover open guard as the attacker resets on top
defensive_options.risk: Mistimed, the roll can hand the attacker your back or deeper rotation

defensive_options.action: Free the trapped leg and flatten your hips to kill the rotation
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker's leg or boot control loosens as they reach for the head
defensive_options.if_successful: The spine realigns and the crank loses its leverage, forcing the attacker to re-set
defensive_options.risk: Slow extraction lets the attacker re-establish boot pressure and rotation

favorable_outcomes.how: Time a granby roll the instant the attacker commits to your head, rolling through the rotation before the chin strap locks to dump them and recover open guard.
Free the trapped leg and flatten your hips to kill the spinal rotation, neutralizing the crank and forcing the attacker to reset their attack from a stalled position.

common_errors.error: Reaching for the attacker's head or grip instead of defending your own neck
common_errors.consequence: Your neck stays exposed and your reaching arm often helps the attacker complete the lever
common_errors.correction: Keep your chin tucked and hand-fight the cranking arm with two-on-one before anything else

common_errors.error: Bridging or exploding while your spine is fully rotated
common_errors.consequence: You add torque to your own cervical spine and accelerate the submission or injury
common_errors.correction: Reduce the rotation first by addressing the leg, then move once your spine is closer to neutral

common_errors.error: Ignoring the trapped leg and focusing only on the upper body
common_errors.consequence: Leg control sustains the rotation, making any upper-body escape impossible
common_errors.correction: Treat the trapped leg as the foundation—extract it to enable spinal realignment

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to tap once the crank is locked
common_errors.consequence: The cervical spine can be injured with very little warning before damage occurs
common_errors.correction: Recognize when escape is gone and tap early—verbally if your hands are trapped

flashcards.question: What is your first priority the moment you feel a neck crank developing?
flashcards.answer: Protect your neck first by tucking your chin hard to your chest and hand-fighting the cranking arm with a two-on-one grip; neck safety comes before any escape attempt.

flashcards.question: Why must you address the trapped leg rather than only fighting the head?
flashcards.answer: The trapped leg and boot pressure are what maintain the spinal rotation that powers the crank; freeing the leg lets you realign your spine and strip the lock of its leverage.

flashcards.question: When is the safest moment to attempt a granby roll escape?
flashcards.answer: Before the chin-strap grip fully locks and while the rotation is still partial; once the grip and full rotation are set, rolling can feed torque into your neck instead of relieving it.

flashcards.question: Why must you tap early to a neck crank rather than trying to ride it out?
flashcards.answer: The cervical spine gives minimal warning before catastrophic failure, so a late tap risks permanent injury; if escape is gone, tap early—verbally if your hands are trapped.

flashcards.question: The opponent threads an arm under your chin—what is your immediate action?
flashcards.answer: Drive your chin to your chest to deny the leverage and clamp a two-on-one on that arm to peel it away before the chin-strap grip can lock around your head.

training_progressions.description: With a compliant partner, practice identifying the cues—the threading arm, the levering head, the building rotation—so you react before the finishing grip is established.
Drill the chin tuck and two-on-one on the cranking arm against light, controlled pressure, building the reflex to protect the neck first under discomfort.
From established Twister Control, practice freeing the trapped leg, flattening to kill rotation, and timing the granby roll with progressive partner resistance.
Defend under controlled live pressure from a partner hunting the crank, working sequential escapes calmly and tapping early the moment escape is no longer viable.
